builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: What the Loss Curve Misses: FP4 Pretraining Slows the Acquisition of Rare Facts
summary: The paper does not propose a replacement technique; it adds rare-fact acquisition measurement (via controlled-exposure synthetic data and gradient statistics) alongside validation loss when evaluating low-precision pretraining recipes such as NVFP4. The cost of ignoring this is hidden: FP4 training can require 1.2–1.5× more data exposures to match BF16 recall of rarely seen facts, a deficit invisible in loss curves and not recoverable by raising the learning rate. The finding can fail to transfer because it derives from small models trained from scratch on synthetic biographies with emulated 4-bit multiplications, so exposure-cost magnitudes at production scale, with native FP4 hardware, or in fine-tuning rather than pretraining remain unverified.
rationale: The reader cannot train foundation models from scratch, so the practical takeaway is limited to preferring BF16/fine-tuning over FP4 training and adding memorization checks when evaluating low-precision APIs, while the full recipe requires unavailable scale.

claims.statement: The paper does not propose a replacement technique; it adds rare-fact acquisition measurement (via controlled-exposure synthetic data and gradient statistics) alongside validation loss when evaluating low-precision pretraining recipes such as NVFP4. The cost of ignoring this is hidden: FP4 training can require 1.2–1.5× more data exposures to match BF16 recall of rarely seen facts, a deficit invisible in loss curves and not recoverable by raising the learning rate. The finding can fail to transfer because it derives from small models trained from scratch on synthetic biographies with emulated 4-bit multiplications, so exposure-cost magnitudes at production scale, with native FP4 hardware, or in fine-tuning rather than pretraining remain unverified.
NVFP4 requires 1.32× and 1.52× as many exposures as BF16 to match rare-fact recall while validation loss differs by only 0.5% and 2%; the exposure cost is about 1.2× at matched loss.
